Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from New Hampshire statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

New Hampshire property tax is assessed and collected at the local level, and owners can appeal an assessment. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Step one: apply in writing to the selectmen or assessors for an abatement by March 1 following the date of notice of tax. (RSA 76:16, I(b); source)
  • Selectmen or assessors must grant or deny the abatement application in writing by July 1 after the notice of tax date; failure to respond is a denial. (RSA 76:16, II; source)
  • If the notice of tax is on or before Dec. 31, the BTLA appeal deadline is September 1 (but no earlier than the municipal decision or July 1); if after Dec. 31, it is 8 months after the notice of tax. (Property Tax | Board of Tax and Land Appeals; source)
  • BTLA appeal filing fee is $65 by check or money order payable to Treasurer, State of NH. (Property Tax | Board of Tax and Land Appeals; source)
  • After 2 years from execution of an unredeemed real estate tax lien, the collector executes a tax deed to the lienholder. (RSA 80:76, I; source)
  • A municipality may refuse a tax deed; the lien then remains indefinitely and the right of redemption continues with interest. (RSA 80:76, II-a, III; source)
Selling in New Hampshire?
We buy New Hampshire houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

How to sell a New Hampshire house when this applies to you

  1. Find out what the closing attorney needs. For an inherited or transferred house, that usually means the recorded deed or the probate paperwork that shows who owns it today.
  2. Get a payoff for any mortgage and the amount of any unpaid property tax. Both are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  3. Compare offers on what you net after repairs, commissions and closing costs, not on the headline price.
  4. If you want a fast, simple closing, ask for a written cash offer. We buy houses as-is, with no repairs and no agent commission. See we buy houses in New Hampshire.

What a cash sale of a New Hampshire house looks like, step by step

People often ask what actually happens after they contact a cash buyer. Here is the usual order of events for a house in New Hampshire.

  1. Tell us about the property. Use the form on this page or call or text (424) 435-2326. We ask about the address, the condition and what is going on, such as a mortgage, back taxes, tenants or an estate.
  2. Get a written cash offer. We review the details and send a written offer. There is no obligation, and you can turn it down and owe us nothing.
  3. Pick your closing date. You choose the timeline. Some owners need weeks to move out, and others want to close quickly.
  4. The title company handles the paperwork. It checks ownership, pays off any mortgage and any unpaid property tax from the proceeds, and records the deed.
  5. You receive the proceeds. Our offers carry no agent commission, no fees and no closing costs to you.

Documents and information to have ready

You do not need everything below to get an offer, but each item makes the sale smoother and helps the title company work faster.

  • The deed or other proof of who owns the property today.
  • A recent mortgage statement or a payoff figure from the lender.
  • The latest property tax bill, plus any notice of unpaid or delinquent tax.
  • Homeowners association details, including dues and any unpaid assessments, if there is an association.
  • Current leases and the tenants' contact information, if the house is rented.
  • Estate paperwork, such as letters from the court, if you inherited the house.
  • A short list of known repairs. We buy as-is, but honest information avoids surprises.

Listing, selling it yourself or a cash offer: how they compare

Listing with an agent can bring a higher headline price when a house is in good shape and you have time. You pay the commission agreed in your listing contract, and you usually handle repairs, showings and the buyer's inspection requests. Closing depends on the buyer's financing.

Selling it yourself saves the listing commission but puts the marketing, the paperwork and the required New Hampshire disclosures on you. You still need a title company or attorney to close.

Taking a cash offer trades some of the headline price for speed and certainty. We buy as-is, so there are no repairs, no showings and no financing contingency. It tends to fit owners dealing with foreclosure pressure, an inherited house, back taxes, tenants or a move on a deadline. Compare every option on what you net after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not on the headline price.

Questions to ask before you sell in New Hampshire

  • Ask the title company what is owed and what the title company will need at closing.
  • Ask your lender for a written payoff figure good through your expected closing date, and ask whether there is a prepayment penalty.
  • Ask the county assessor whether a pending appeal or exemption affects the bill, and whether any exemption you receive ends when you sell.
  • If the house was inherited, ask the title company which court documents it needs before it will insure the sale.
  • If tenants live in the house, check the lease for its end date and any notice you must give.

These are general questions to start a conversation, not legal advice. Rules in New Hampshire change, so confirm details with the official office or a New Hampshire attorney or tax professional.

More questions about selling in New Hampshire

How fast can I close on a cash sale?

You choose the closing date within what the title company needs to clear ownership and payoffs.

Do I have to clean out or repair the house?

No. We buy houses as-is, so you do not need to make repairs before selling.

Will you buy a house that has tenants in it?

Yes. We buy rentals as-is, occupied or vacant. Tell us about the lease when you request an offer.

What if I owe more on the mortgage than the house is worth?

Tell us the payoff figure. A sale that does not cover the loan may need lender approval, so ask your lender about a short sale before you sign anything.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate is finished?

It depends on who has legal authority to sign. The title company can tell you what court paperwork it needs.

Is there any cost to request an offer?

No. Requesting an offer is free and carries no obligation.

What happens to unpaid property tax when I sell?

The closing agent pays unpaid tax from the sale proceeds at closing.

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from New Hampshire statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

New Hampshire evictions follow notice and court steps set by state law. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • For residential tenancies, 30 days' eviction notice suffices; 7 days if the reason is nonpayment, substantial damage, behavior affecting health/safety, or domestic violence cotenant termination. (RSA 540:3, II; source)
  • Notice must state the reason with specificity; nonpayment notices must advise of the right to cure under RSA 540:9. (RSA 540:3, III-IV; source)
  • Restricted property may be terminated only for listed reasons including nonpayment, substantial damage, material lease violation, other good cause, and lease expiration with 60 days' notice for leases of 12 months or longer. (RSA 540:2, II; source)
  • After the notice expires the landlord obtains a landlord-tenant writ; the return day is 7 days from service; if the tenant appears a hearing is set within 10 days. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Tenant may cure nonpayment by paying back rent plus $15, up to three times in 12 months; money judgments in these cases are limited to $1500. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • Court may stay the writ of possession up to 90 days if the tenant pays rent weekly; notice of intent to appeal is due within 7 days of the notice of judgment. (Navigating the NH Eviction Process | NH Judicial Branch; source)
  • A refusal of a rent increase noticed 30 days ahead, and legitimate business or economic reasons, can constitute 'other good cause' for terminating a restricted tenancy. (RSA 540:2, IV-V; source)
  • For residential tenancies, 30 days' eviction notice is generally required. (RSA 540:3, II; source)
  • Lease expiration is a ground only for leases of 12 months or longer, with 60 days' written notice and possessory action filed within 6 months. (RSA 540:2, II(i); source)

Last updated November 14, 2026. Citations come from New Hampshire statutes and official agency pages linked in Sources. Where we could not confirm something on an official page, we say so.

New Hampshire probate runs through the courts named in the sources below. Here is what the official sources say.

What the official sources say

  • Waiver of Administration under RSA 553:32 is a simplified probate process for testate or intestate estates; no inventory, fiduciary bond or accounting is required. (What is Waiver of Administration? | NH Judicial Branch; source)
